title: Helix 12 and Tissue Helpers: Turning the Switch

scenes.visual: Title card on deep slate background matching the first film: 'Helix 12 and Tissue Helpers: Turning the Switch' in crisp white (size 48). Below, the teal ligand-binding pocket from the first film rests with its hinged helix-12 bar gently swaying.

scenes.tts: The first film showed one nuclear receptor binding both ligand and D N A. How does a tiny molecule inside the pocket flip a gene from off to on? And why can one drug block estrogen in breast tissue yet imitate it in the uterus?
scenes.caption: The first film showed one nuclear receptor binding both ligand and DNA. How does a tiny molecule inside the pocket flip a gene from off to on? And why can one drug block estrogen in breast tissue yet imitate it in the uterus?
scenes.visual: Opens on the exact teal receptor sitting on pale cream DNA from the end of the first film, carrying the warm orange AF-1 block on the left and the teal pocket on the right. As the two questions are asked, the camera zooms smoothly into the teal ligand pocket while two small badges pulse gently at the top right: 'Breast: OFF' (coral-red) and 'Uterus: ON' (emerald-green), size 28.
scenes.narration: The first film showed one nuclear receptor binding both ligand and DNA. How does a tiny molecule inside the pocket flip a gene from off to on? And why can one drug block estrogen in breast tissue yet imitate it in the uterus?

scenes.tts: Zoom into the hormone-binding domain, built from about twelve helices around a hydrophobic pocket. Its last helix, helix twelve, is the main moving part. When an agonist like estradiol enters, it switches the receptor on. Helix twelve folds shut across the mouth of the pocket like a lid.
scenes.caption: Zoom into the hormone-binding domain, built from about 12 helices around a hydrophobic pocket. Its last helix, helix 12, is the main moving part. When an agonist like estradiol enters, it switches the receptor on. Helix 12 folds shut across the mouth of the pocket like a lid.
scenes.visual: The teal hormone-binding domain fills 65% of the frame height as a clean cutaway schematic of bundled tubes forming an inner pocket (no molecular structure). The outermost bar on a hinge glows bright teal and is labelled 'Helix 12' (size 30). A gold sphere labelled 'Estradiol (agonist)' glides into the pocket, and helix 12 swings smoothly across the opening like a closing lid.
scenes.narration: Zoom into the hormone-binding domain, built from about 12 helices around a hydrophobic pocket. Its last helix, helix 12, is the main moving part. When an agonist like estradiol enters, it switches the receptor on. Helix 12 folds shut across the mouth of the pocket like a lid.

scenes.tts: Closed like that, helix twelve completes a shallow surface groove called A F two. Co-activators carry a short helix that fits it. Docked co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl tags to histones, the spools D N A wraps around. The D N A loosens, and R N A polymerase starts copying the gene.
scenes.caption: Closed like that, helix 12 completes a shallow surface groove called AF-2. Co-activators carry a short helix that fits it. Docked co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl tags to histones, the spools DNA wraps around. The DNA loosens, and RNA polymerase starts copying the gene.
scenes.visual: As helix 12 clicks shut, a glowing notch forms on the domain's surface labelled 'AF-2 groove' (size 30). An emerald-green co-activator block slides in and seats a short green rod labelled 'LXXLL' neatly into the AF-2 groove. Below, emerald acetyl dots land on pale cream histone spools, which slide apart so a bright RNA strand begins extending from the DNA.
scenes.narration: Closed like that, helix 12 completes a shallow surface groove called AF-2. Co-activators carry a short helix that fits it. Docked co-activators bring enzymes that add acetyl tags to histones, the spools DNA wraps around. The DNA loosens, and RNA polymerase starts copying the gene.

scenes.tts: An antagonist fills the same pocket without switching the receptor on. The liver converts the breast-cancer drug tamoxifen into tighter-binding forms like four-hydroxytamoxifen. It fits the pocket, but one long side chain sticks out of the opening.
scenes.caption: An antagonist fills the same pocket without switching the receptor on. The liver converts the breast-cancer drug tamoxifen into tighter-binding forms like 4-hydroxytamoxifen. It fits the pocket, but one long side chain sticks out of the opening.
scenes.visual: The gold estradiol and emerald co-activator glide out, and helix 12 swings back open. A coral-red shape with a prominent protruding arm, labelled '4-hydroxytamoxifen' (size 28), enters the same teal pocket. Its bulky red arm juts clearly out of the pocket mouth, physically occupying the exact path where helix 12 previously closed.
scenes.narration: An antagonist fills the same pocket without switching the receptor on. The liver converts the breast-cancer drug tamoxifen into tighter-binding forms like 4-hydroxytamoxifen. It fits the pocket, but one long side chain sticks out of the opening.

scenes.tts: That protruding side chain sits right where helix twelve wants to fold shut. Notice the nearby notch where co-activators dock. If helix twelve cannot close, what happens to that groove?
scenes.caption: That protruding side chain sits right where helix 12 wants to fold shut. Notice the nearby notch where co-activators dock. If helix 12 cannot close, what happens to that groove?
scenes.visual: The teal helix-12 bar nudges gently against the protruding coral-red side arm and bounces back, unable to shut. A dotted outline highlights the nearby surface groove ('Co-activator groove', size 28) while an emerald co-activator hovers waiting outside.
scenes.narration: That protruding side chain sits right where helix 12 wants to fold shut. Notice the nearby notch where co-activators dock. If helix 12 cannot close, what happens to that groove?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic pocket with the coral side arm blocking the mouth and the question card at top center: 'Helix 12 cannot close. What happens to the groove?' (size 34). A smooth 4.5-second timer bar fills along the bottom while helix 12 hovers.

scenes.tts: The receptor's own helix takes the groove, because helix twelve cannot close as a lid. Instead it swings around and lies inside the co-activator groove itself. That turns the lid into a plug. With the A F two groove occupied, co-activators cannot bind there, so breast cells keep the gene off.
scenes.caption: The receptor's own helix takes the groove, because helix 12 cannot close as a lid. Instead it swings around and lies inside the co-activator groove itself. That turns the lid into a plug. With the AF-2 groove occupied, co-activators cannot bind there, so breast cells keep the gene off.
scenes.visual: Helix 12 swings smoothly around and settles lengthwise right inside the AF-2 groove, flashing with the label 'Helix 12 blocks AF-2' (size 30). The waiting emerald co-activator approaches, bumps harmlessly against the occupied groove, and drifts away as the DNA spools tighten below.
scenes.narration: The receptor's own helix takes the groove, because helix 12 cannot close as a lid. Instead it swings around and lies inside the co-activator groove itself. That turns the lid into a plug. With the AF-2 groove occupied, co-activators cannot bind there, so breast cells keep the gene off.

scenes.tts: Yet tamoxifen still lets the receptor pair on D N A, leaving a second switching surface exposed. That front-end surface, A F one, does not depend on helix twelve. So the outcome can depend on the helper proteins each tissue makes. Cells rich in co-activators that work through A F one can read the same drug as on.
scenes.caption: Yet tamoxifen still lets the receptor pair on DNA, leaving a second switching surface exposed. That front-end surface, AF-1, does not depend on helix 12. So the outcome can depend on the helper proteins each tissue makes. Cells rich in co-activators that work through AF-1 can read the same drug as on.
scenes.visual: The camera pulls back to show the full teal receptor paired on DNA with the coral drug locked inside and AF-2 plugged, while the warm orange block on the left glows bright ('AF-1 still open', size 30). The frame splits into two schematic cells: left labelled 'Breast' (mostly coral co-repressors docking, DNA staying tight, 'OFF') and right labelled 'Uterus' (abundant emerald co-activators docking via orange AF-1, DNA loosening, 'ON').
scenes.narration: Yet tamoxifen still lets the receptor pair on DNA, leaving a second switching surface exposed. That front-end surface, AF-1, does not depend on helix 12. So the outcome can depend on the helper proteins each tissue makes. Cells rich in co-activators that work through AF-1 can read the same drug as on.

scenes.tts: That helps explain why tamoxifen opposes estrogen in breast tissue yet imitates it in uterus and bone. Either way, the receptor works through new R N A and protein, unlike fast cyclic A M P relays. The first new messenger R N A appears within tens of minutes, and protein changes build over hours.
scenes.caption: That helps explain why tamoxifen opposes estrogen in breast tissue yet imitates it in uterus and bone. Either way, the receptor works through new RNA and protein, unlike fast cyclic AMP relays. The first new messenger RNA appears within tens of minutes, and protein changes build over hours.
scenes.visual: The split cells slide gently into the upper half as a clean 'Schematic timeline' (size 28) unfolds across the lower half. A rapid spike curve labelled 'cAMP: seconds' rises and falls at the left; beside it, a teal curve ('New mRNA: tens of min') and a broader emerald curve ('New protein: hours') rise slowly across the right.
scenes.narration: That helps explain why tamoxifen opposes estrogen in breast tissue yet imitates it in uterus and bone. Either way, the receptor works through new RNA and protein, unlike fast cyclic AMP relays. The first new messenger RNA appears within tens of minutes, and protein changes build over hours.

scenes.tts: In return, those new proteins remain after the hormone clears, and one receptor can reset many genes together. A drug is not simply on or off by itself. Ligand shape and each cell's helpers decide whether genes turn on.

scenes.visual: On the schematic timeline, a small gold hormone bar fades out while the broad emerald protein plateau stays elevated ('Proteins outlast hormone', size 28). Above, the teal pocket (showing ligand shape) and the emerald/coral helper blocks glow in balance over the cream DNA strand.
